processing: Black tea made as gongfu strips in the mid-century state farm era; Guizhou also developed broken black teas for export.
harvest_season: Little is documented for the historical tea; Guizhou black teas today are mostly made from spring leaf.
appearance_dry: Dark, fine twisted strips, as is typical of gongfu black tea.
appearance_liquor: Clear bright red-amber, typical of gongfu black teas.
taste_profile: No detailed tasting record survives for the historical brand; Guizhou gongfu teas today tend to be clean, sweet and fairly brisk.

brewing.notes: A general gongfu starting point. It also works Western-style, 3 g to 200 ml for about three minutes.

vintage_note: Today the name is used loosely for Guizhou black tea, sold as a recent harvest. Named appellations such as Zunyi Hong or Pu'an Hong tell you far more, and the old export brand is history rather than something you can buy by year.
description:
Qian is the old short name for Guizhou, so Qian Hong means Guizhou black tea. It began as a brand name from the state tea farm at Meitan and is now used more loosely for the province's black teas.

The farm made gongfu black tea by hand and early machine, in strips, and the province's research institute later developed broken grades too. Modern drinkers are more likely to meet its descendants than the original.

As with other gongfu black teas of Guizhou, expect a clean, sweet cup with some briskness. It forgives a longer steep better than delicate Fujian bud teas.

If a bag says only Qian Hong, ask where in the province it comes from. Zunyi Hong and Pu'an Hong are the better-defined teas to try next.
history:
The story starts in Meitan during the war. In 1940 Liu Ganzhi led a successful trial of black tea at the Meitan experimental tea farm and called it Mei Hong; tea expert Feng Shaoqiu compared its fine, even leaf favourably with Keemun.

Wu Xiancai began working on gongfu black tea at the state Meitan farm in 1952, and about two years later the farm's Qian Hong brand was selling abroad through Shanghai and Guangzhou. Exports from the farm ran at 10,000 to 20,000 dan a year until the 1970s, though some later accounts blur Mei Hong and Qian Hong together.
